cards.front: A {{c1::trait}} is a feature such as colour, shape or height.
cards.quote: A trait is a feature such as colour, shape or height.

cards.front: A {{c1::population}} is a group of the same kind of living thing in one area.
cards.quote: A population is a group of the same kind of living thing in one area.

cards.front: In a population of one kind of living thing, what does variation mean?
cards.back: Differences among the members of the population.
cards.quote: Variation means differences among its members.

cards.front: The leaves on one white oak tree share nearly the same DNA but still differ in size. Where do the differences come from?
cards.back: From growth conditions and chance during growth, since the leaves share nearly the same inherited DNA.
cards.quote: Leaves on one oak share nearly the same inherited DNA, so their differences come from growth conditions and chance during growth.

cards.front: What are the two main sources of variation in many traits, such as height?
cards.back: Inheritance (alleles from parents) and the environment (conditions and experiences while growing). Height uses both.
cards.quote: Height uses both: many genes, plus childhood food and health.

cards.front: A {{c1::mutation}} is a change in the DNA sequence, the order of the bases.
cards.quote: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence, the order of the bases.
cards.section: Mutation adds a new genetic difference

cards.front: How is a mutation different from reshuffling of alleles when sex cells form?
cards.back: Reshuffling only mixes alleles the parents already have. A mutation can make a new allele.
cards.quote: Reshuffling mixes alleles the parents already have. A mutation can make a new allele.
cards.section: Mutation adds a new genetic difference

cards.front: Name three things that can cause a mutation.
cards.back: Copying mistakes before a cell divides, radiation such as ultraviolet light from the Sun, and some chemicals.
cards.quote: Causes include copying mistakes before a cell divides, radiation such as ultraviolet light from the Sun, and some chemicals.
cards.section: Mutation adds a new genetic difference

cards.front: Why can a mutation in a gene change how a living thing works?
cards.back: Many genes code for a protein, so a mutation can change that protein or how much of it a cell makes. Sometimes the protein works the same as before.
cards.quote: So a mutation can change that protein or how much of it a cell makes.
cards.section: Mutation adds a new genetic difference

cards.front: Mutations are {{c1::random}}: they happen by chance, not because a living thing needs their effect.
cards.quote: Mutations are random: they happen by chance, not because a living thing needs their effect.
cards.section: Mutation adds a new genetic difference

cards.front: A hiker gets a mutation in some skin cells on her arm from strong sunlight. Will her future children inherit it from those cells? Why or why not?
cards.back: No. Skin cells are body cells, and in animals a body-cell mutation stays in that one body.
cards.quote: in people and other animals a body-cell mutation stays in that one body, but a sex-cell mutation can be passed to offspring.

cards.front: In a mouse, radiation causes a mutation in one sperm cell, and that sperm helps make a pup. Can the pup inherit the mutation?
cards.back: Yes. Sperm are sex cells, and a mutation in a sex cell can reach offspring.
cards.quote: A mutation in a sex cell can reach offspring.

cards.front: Knowing that a mutation is in a sex cell tells you it can be passed on. Does it tell you whether the mutation helps or harms?
cards.back: No. Where a mutation goes does not tell us what it does.
cards.quote: Where a mutation goes does not tell us what it does.

cards.front: In the recipe comparison, what are the three possible effects of a mutation, and where does the comparison stop working?
cards.back: Many change little, some harm, a few help, perhaps in only one environment. A recipe has a writer, but no one chooses a mutation.
cards.quote: Many misprints change little, some spoil the dish, and a few make it better, perhaps only in one kitchen.
cards.section: Helpful, harmful or neither: test the claim

cards.front: In a lab, one E. coli mutant grows best on one food. The food is changed. Must the same mutant still grow best?
cards.back: No. Which mutant grew best changed when the food changed, so a mutation's effect often depends on the environment.
cards.quote: In the bacteria study, which mutant grew best changed when the food changed.

cards.front: In the CDC reference for girls just over 12, the 5th percentile is 139.2 cm and the 95th is 163.5 cm. How wide is the spread of the middle 90 percent?
cards.back: 163.5 - 139.2 = 24.3 cm. This is 0.3 cm less than the boys' spread of 24.6 cm.
cards.quote: This is how widely the middle 90 percent of boys in the reference spread.

cards.front: In the CDC reference for children just over 12, the 50th-percentile height is 149.3 cm for boys and 151.5 cm for girls. Which is greater, and by how much?
cards.quote: 151.5 − 149.3 = 2.2 centimetres, with the girls' value greater.

cards.front: In a height reference table, what does a 25th-percentile height mean?
cards.back: About 25 percent of children in the reference were that height or shorter.
cards.quote: A 25th-percentile height means about 25 percent of children in the reference were that height or shorter.

cards.front: A student says the 24.6 cm spread in boys' heights explains why one boy in her class is tall. Is she right?
cards.back: No. The spread shows how widely the middle 90 percent of boys vary. It does not explain one child's height.
cards.quote: It does not explain one child's height.

cards.front: A class grows bacteria in 5 dishes with no antibiotic, then adds the drug. Resistant colonies per dish are 0, 0, 12, 0 and 2. Does this fit chance mutations before the drug, or the drug causing the mutations?
cards.back: Chance mutations before the drug. An early change can leave many resistant descendants in one dish while another gets none. If the drug caused them, every dish would give similar small counts.
cards.quote: An early change can leave many resistant descendants in one dish, while another dish gets none.

cards.front: In a study of white oak leaf length, why compare the sunny and shady sides of the same tree instead of two different trees?
cards.back: The tree's genes are the same on both sides, so a difference in length points to the environment.
cards.quote: Control: comparing the two sides of the same tree, so the tree's genes are the same.

cards.front: On one oak, sunny-side leaves are clearly longer than shady-side leaves, yet leaves on each side also differ from one another. What does each result show?
cards.back: The difference between sides shows the environment affects leaf length. The spread within each side shows variation even with the same genes.
cards.quote: The spread within each side shows variation even with the same genes.

cards.front: A mutation in an egg cell of a beetle gives some offspring a new colour. Can you say whether the new colour will help them survive?
cards.back: No. It can pass on because it is in a sex cell, but it may or may not help survival, and the effect depends on the environment. It arose by chance.
cards.quote: That variation may or may not help an individual survive and reproduce.
cards.section: Helpful, harmful or neither: test the claim
